summary: Defines changes to the DNS to support renumberable and aggregatable IPv6 addressing. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo proposed a new way for the Internet's address book to store IPv6 addresses. Instead of putting a whole address in one record, it split the address into pieces and chained them together, which made it easier to renumber a network. The idea did not last; RFC 2874 is now Historic.

questions: how does a6 record chaining work
subtitle: A now-Historic plan to store IPv6 addresses in the DNS as chains of prefix records, so whole networks could be renumbered.

tldr.problem: In IPv4, keeping address information in the DNS was one of the obstacles to renumbering sites and providers, and storing each whole IPv6 address in a single record would repeat the problem.
tldr.mechanism: A new A6 record holds part of an IPv6 address, a prefix length and the name of another record that supplies the leading bits. Reverse lookups use bit-string labels and DNAME records under IP6.ARPA.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2874 was proposed as a replacement for RFC 1886, but it is now marked Historic and has been updated by later RFCs.

facts.label: Recommended delegation
facts.value: One or two levels until more experience is gained

today: RFC 2874 is marked Historic. It updated RFC 1886 and has itself been updated by RFC 3152, RFC 3226, RFC 3363 and RFC 3364, so the A6 scheme it describes should not be treated as current.

sections.title: Why Renumbering Needed New DNS Records
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a problem in IPv4: keeping address information in the DNS was one of the obstacles that made site and provider renumbering hard. To store IPv6 addresses without making renumbering harder, the memo defines four extensions.

  • A new record type, A6, maps a name to an IPv6 address, with indirection for the leading prefix bits.
  • Queries that gather IPv4 addresses in the additional section are redefined to gather IPv6 addresses too.
  • A new domain, IP6.ARPA, supports lookups based on an IPv6 address.
  • A new prefix-delegation method uses bit-string labels and DNAME records.

The memo describes itself as a replacement for RFC 1886 and a departure from current practice, and expects that RFC 1886 will become Historic after a reasonable period.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo set out to make the Internet's address book easy to update when a whole neighborhood changes its numbers. It adds one new kind of record for addresses and a new place to look up addresses in reverse.

sections.title: The A6 Record
sections.content:
The A6 record is specific to the IN class and has type number 38. Its data holds two or three fields: a prefix length (one octet, valued 0 to 128), an address suffix (exactly enough octets to hold 128 minus the prefix length bits, with 0 to 7 zero pad bits), and a prefix name encoded as a domain name that MUST NOT be compressed.

The name is absent when the prefix length is zero, and the suffix is absent when the prefix length is 128. A prefix length of zero means the record holds all the significant leading bits of a complete address; otherwise the name points to other A6 records that supply the leading bits. The RFC suggests that a record used as a prefix keep its insignificant trailing bits set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: An A6 record is like a card with the last part of an address and a pointer to the card that holds the first part. Its prefix length says how much of the address this card covers.

sections.title: Building an Address from A6 Chains
sections.content:
To find the addresses of a name, a DNS client MUST obtain one or more complete chains of A6 records. A chain begins with a record owned by the name, includes a record owned by that record's prefix name, and continues until it reaches a record with a prefix length of zero. Each bit of the address is taken from the earliest record in the chain that validly covers that position. Records with more than one A6 record at a level multiply the number of addresses formed.

It is an error for a record with prefix length L1 to name a domain that owns a record with a larger prefix length L2; the offending record with the larger length MUST be ignored. A query for A6 also causes NS additional section processing for the prefix names. If some queries fail, a client can receive a non-empty but incomplete set of addresses, which the RFC says may be acceptable in many cases.

Existing query types that return address data in the additional section (NS, MX, MB, AFSDB and RT) are redefined to return A, A6 and AAAA data, with A highest priority and AAAA lowest. Resolvers must limit the work and the number of DNS requests generated per lookup.
sections.plainLanguage: To reach the whole address, a program follows the pointers from card to card until it finds one that needs no more, then joins the pieces in order. One name can lead to several addresses because more than one card can fit at a step.

sections.title: Reverse Lookups under IP6.ARPA
sections.content:
Lookups keyed on an IPv6 address use a bit-string label, a compact way to write an arbitrary string of bits as a sequence of one-bit domain labels. That lets records sit at any bit boundary. In the RFC's notation, the hexadecimal digits inside \[x3FFE07C0004000090A0020FFFE812B32/128].IP6.ARPA. name a full 128-bit address.

Delegation uses DNAME records, which redirect a whole subtree of names rather than a single name, instead of zone cuts and NS records. The RFC says all address space delegations SHOULD use DNAME, and suggests keeping address and prefix data directly below a label IP6. To find the name for an address, a client sends a PTR query with QCLASS=IN for the bit-string name under IP6.ARPA, then follows the DNAME and NS records it gets back.

Because a zone is reached through DNAME, one zone can serve several parallel copies of an address space, such as a multihomed site, and it survives renumbering unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: To find who owns an address, the query is sent backward, one piece at a time. Each step points to a smaller office with the next piece, until a record names the host.

sections.title: Transition from RFC 1886 and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
Long chains need more records and more lookups, and those records usually come from different zones that can fail independently. The records can exceed the space in a UDP response, and DNS Security checking costs more when different signature chains must be verified. Until more experience is gained, the RFC recommends limiting prefix delegations to one or two levels, starting with none and moving to a single level within one zone.

To work with resolvers that only know AAAA records, a zone can generate AAAA records from its A6 data. A generated AAAA record's TTL MUST be no more than the minimum TTL of the A6 records used to form it, and it MUST be signed if the zone is secure. A client MAY be configurable about the order of A6 and AAAA queries, but the default MUST be to try A6 first, then AAAA.

For reverse lookups, RFC 1886 used nibble labels under IP6.INT. During a transition, the RFC recommends that implementations first look up the binary label in IP6.ARPA and, if that fails, try the nibble label in IP6.INT.
sections.plainLanguage: While people switch to the new address book, the old one keeps working alongside it, and lookups check the new one first. To keep things simple at first, the memo advises only a level or two of chained records.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The signing authority for the A6 records that determine an IPv6 address is spread among the entities along its delegation path. DNS Security applies fully to bit-string labels and DNAME records, and, as in IPv4, checking name-to-address mappings is logically independent of checking address-to-name mappings.

With or without DNSSEC, the incomplete but non-empty address set could be caused by selective interference with lookups. If that would be worse than a complete failure, a client could refuse to act on an incomplete set, or a server could list all addresses in A6 records with prefix length zero. IANA assigned the A6 resource record the type value 38.
sections.plainLanguage: Because an address is assembled from many cards, an attacker who hides one card could mislead a client. A client can protect itself by refusing to act unless it has the complete set.

viz.caption: THE TWO OR THREE PARTS OF A6 RECORD DATA (RFC 2874)

cells: Value 0 to 128; the name is absent when it is 0
Holds 128 minus prefix length bits, plus 0 to 7 zero pad bits; absent when prefix length is 128
A domain name that MUST NOT be compressed
